The IP Address Wasn’t the Interesting Part

Adam Rhys Heaton September 22, 2026
DPRK WaterPlum Threat Intelligence Attribution Laptop Farms

Japan just dismantled its first confirmed North Korean IT-worker laptop farm.

That alone makes the case interesting. But after reading through the reporting, that wasn't the part that caught my attention.

It was the IP addresses.

Japanese authorities and their international partners reported that WaterPlum actors and North Korean IT workers had been observed using some of the same IP addresses. Those addresses showed up in activity involving laptop farms, crowdsourcing services, and job applications.

That's a useful connection.

It's also exactly the kind of evidence that can get analysts into trouble if we ask it to prove too much.

A shared IP doesn't tell me that two activities were performed by the same person. It doesn't prove ownership of the infrastructure, and it certainly doesn't mean everything coming through that address belongs in one bucket.

What it gives us is a relationship.

And in this case, there are a lot of other relationships sitting around it.

Why the laptop farm matters

The term laptop farm makes the operation sound more exotic than it really is.

Strip away the North Korea angle for a second and the problem being solved is fairly straightforward: someone physically located in one place needs to look like an employee working from somewhere else.

If you're trying to maintain that fiction over weeks or months, logging in from the wrong country every morning is going to become a problem.

So you put the computer where the employee is supposed to be and operate it remotely.

That's the interesting part of the infrastructure to me. The laptop isn't simply an indicator we can add to a list. It's there because the operation requires it.

The multinational advisory describes facilitators hosting computers and servers that North Korean workers could access remotely. That allowed workers outside the claimed location to operate through equipment that appeared much more consistent with where their employer expected them to be.

Once you look at it that way, the question changes.

Instead of asking, What IP should I block?

I want to know, What does this operation need in order to keep working?

IP addresses are disposable.

The need to hide the operator's real geography isn't.

That distinction is useful because dependencies tend to survive longer than individual indicators.

A bad interview tells us more than you might think

One case in the Japanese reporting makes this much easier to see.

In May 2025, a Japanese cryptocurrency exchange received an application from someone authorities later associated with this activity.

There were problems with the application, but not the kind where you could point to one thing and say, "There it is."

The applicant used a VPN. That's hardly remarkable by itself.

The résumé claimed experience across a very broad collection of programming languages, blockchain technologies, cryptocurrency systems, and cloud platforms. Suspicious? Maybe. Proof of anything? No.

The person's claimed background was complicated too. The applicant said they were born in Malaysia, lived in Finland, and spoke Malay and Chinese natively. During the interview, however, parts of the story apparently didn't hold together. English proficiency didn't fit particularly well with the education and professional history being presented, and the applicant had trouble discussing some of the technical skills listed on the résumé.

Again, none of this is a North Korean IT-worker detector.

That's important.

Someone having a terrible technical interview does not make them a state actor. Neither does using a VPN. Neither does an unusual résumé.

What makes this case useful is that the problems weren't all in the same place.

The claimed identity said one thing.

The résumé said another.

The interview raised additional questions.

The network activity added another layer.

Then there was the infrastructure.

At some point we're no longer looking at a weird résumé or an odd IP address. We're looking at different parts of the same story failing to agree with one another.

That's a very different analytical problem.

We tend to scatter the evidence ourselves

This is also where I think defenders make life unnecessarily difficult.

Think about where these observations normally live inside a company.

Recruiting has the résumé.

The hiring manager remembers that strange interview.

Identity has account information.

Network security has the VPN and IP telemetry.

Endpoint security sees remote-access software or unusual host activity.

Finance knows where the money is being sent.

Maybe fraud has another piece.

Nobody necessarily has the whole thing.

From each team's perspective, what they're seeing may not be enough to justify much action. A VPN? Fine. An awkward interview? Happens every day. Remote-access software? Depends on the environment. An unusual payment request? Send it to somebody else.

The attacker gets an advantage because we've divided one operation into six organizational problems.

That is why I keep coming back to contradiction rather than individual indicators.

The Japanese case included other behaviors as well: avoiding in-person meetings, requests involving cryptocurrency payments, applicants repeatedly looking toward another screen, unexplained voices during interviews, audio and video problems, and even the use of AI face-swapping.

I wouldn't write a detection rule that says someone looking away from their webcam is a North Korean IT worker. That would be absurd.

But imagine the same applicant is supposedly in Finland, connects through questionable infrastructure, can't explain the technologies on the résumé, has strange behavior during the interview, wants an unusual payment arrangement, and later has remote-access activity that doesn't fit the story.

Now I care.

Not because any one signal became magically reliable.

Because the signals started disagreeing with the same claim.

Back to that shared IP

This is why the shared IP observation deserves attention without being overstated.

WaterPlum activity and North Korean IT-worker activity appearing behind the same addresses establishes a technical relationship. By itself, that relationship has limits.

In this case, however, it doesn't exist by itself.

Japanese and partner agencies also documented the laptop-farm infrastructure, job applications, remote access, interview behavior, identity issues, financial activity, and other operational details. The National Police Agency of Japan and FBI further assess that WaterPlum actors and some North Korean IT workers operate under the 313 General Bureau of North Korea's Munitions Industry Department.

Now the shared IP has context.

That's the difference.

If all I had was:

same IP = same actor

I'd be very uncomfortable with the conclusion.

But that's not the evidence package here.

What we're really looking at is shared infrastructure appearing alongside an operational need, overlapping activity, investigative findings, identity discrepancies and government attribution.

The IP address didn't solve the attribution.

It became useful because of everything around it.

This is bigger than DPRK IT workers

There's a broader lesson here for threat intelligence.

We love indicators because they're easy to handle.

Put the hash in the EDR.

Put the domain in the blocklist.

Search the SIEM for the IP.

Add it to the TIP.

Done.

Except the actor changes the domain tomorrow.

What usually changes much more slowly is the problem the actor has to solve.

If someone needs to impersonate a remote employee, they have to establish a believable identity.

They need to appear to be where they claim to be.

They need to get through an interview.

They need a device.

They need access to that device.

Eventually, they need to get paid.

Every one of those requirements creates another place where the story can break.

That's what I find useful about the Japanese laptop-farm case. Yes, there are new indicators. Yes, there's another piece of infrastructure defenders can look for.

But the more durable takeaway isn't an IP address.

It's that deception has dependencies, and dependencies leave evidence in different places.

The trick is getting those places to talk to one another.
